stories.title_en: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)

comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB.  EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.
https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/
As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it.  But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.
You should probably assume that, if you are running anything that can be convinced to use this API to encode a very long blob as base64, then you are in trouble. I don’t know why a modern server would do this.
BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs.  Stay away.
edit: Fixed my size threshold, hopefully. I was thinking of unsigned ints, but this is a
signed
int. I have not looked at the code, just the description.

comments.author: userbinator
comments.text:
I think CVSS 9.8 is exaggerated. This is not remotely anywhere near as serious as Heartbleed. It's an internal function which will fail if its input is far too long, but exploitability rests on how untrusted input can reach it; the key word being "untrusted". E.g. if you operate a base64 encoding service on the Internet that just reads all the data into memory at once and calls EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's exploitable. If you have a protocol that involves a block of data with a 16-bit length field which is passed to EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's 100% safe.
For those wondering about TLS: speaking as someone who has written a TLS implementation, AFAIK neither base64 encoding nor decoding occurs in the protocol itself, and the longest length field is 24 bits (Hello stream). Certificate processing involves ASN.1 which does support arbitrarily-long integers, but that's a big hint to check that they're within a sensical range.

comments.author: synapsomorphy
comments.text:
Sokoban is cool, but far from the most interesting thing here, which is the design of experiment factories for verifiable domains.
The base building blocks you need to make this work:
- dataset
- unhackable success metric
- hardened, isolated f(dataset, solver) -> metric
- helps a ton but not required: human with strong intuitive domain understanding
This is exactly the kind of RL environment in which the models are forged, so they're truly excellent at basically all stages of this process.
I'm working on something similar for image and video compression. The SOTA approach for these things currently is mostly deep neural networks. But agent powered experiment factories let you cover FAR more ground in algorithm-space than before, which makes deterministic and explicit algorithms, with little or no heuristics (aka floating point weights) feasible once again.
Explicit algorithms (SGD) grew implicit ones (neural nets) that are more powerful and general, but also more opaque and less efficient. Now those implicit ones have made search over explicit algorithms vastly faster, which is making them increasingly competitive with neural methods.

comments.author: jzelinskie
comments.text:
I haven't used these extensions, but I like the direction of being able to extend Postgres by tailing its own internals (pg_squeeze approach) than triggers (pg_repack).
We (the SpiceDB developers) took a similar approach to solve a different problem a few years ago: implementing strict serializability in Postgres[0]. By hooking into the transactions layer themselves (pg_xact), we could layer on our own MVCC reusing the real Postgres transactions to compute visibility and total ordering. When you can just tail the Postgres internals, you don't even need to implement a Postgres extension, which can keep it portable across locked-down, managed Postgres offerings.
Do folks know of other clever implementations of behavior by "spying" on the Postgres internals?
[0]:
https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_f6fHy4DWWM

comments.author: FinnLobsien
comments.text:
AI and LLMs, in my opinion, are effectively the industrialization of knowledge work.
Like it or not, industrialization brought many benefits and we couldn't imagine our modern way of living without it (just think about medicines). Industrial production made so many things so much more accessible for so many people.
But an industrialist perspective doesn't care about the process of making stuff, only about the outcome. The shoemakers deep knowledge of leathers, his intuition of all sorts of different shoes, and the pride of that competence—that doesn't matter when you can make thousands of shoes a day that cost 0.5% of something artisanal. The people working at the shoe factory only carry things to and fro and occasionally fix some machine issue.
This has tons of benefits and tons of downsides. But with physical goods, a shoe is a shoe.
With knowledge work like writing, the process is often the entire point. The point of writing a paper is what you learned in the process. The point of documented software architecture is to develop an understanding deep enough to drive coherent downstream decisions. If those things are no longer true, the asset it stands for is basically worthless.

AI behaves like a constraint solver. You put in the right set of constraints (on writing style, on technical details, on structure) and with a sufficiently capable model what will come out is a close approximation of something you might have produced, or at least something you might have been happy to receive from someone else. There will usually be aspects that aren’t quite right, so you add more constraints.
If you have a job/life where there are more things you want/need to achieve than you have time for, this can be a significant accelerant.
It does require the ability to judge when something is good enough of course.
This is actually no different to leading teams of humans. You guide individuals and set the standards and take responsibility for the output of the team.

comments.author: cadamsdotcom
comments.text:
It's an oversimplification to equate the leveraging of external intelligence with not thinking for yourself.
External intelligence will get you out of a ton of intellectual grunt work so you are freed to think at a higher level. You've are freed to think about different things more core to your problem, and if you wield the tools well you can choose what you offload. But it should be viewed as a tool not a shortcut...
Consider an accountant summing numbers with a calculator vs. by hand. There's way less thinking needed to get the numbers summed right. But blindly summing numbers doesn't make the work correct even if the sums are correct...
No one should put their name on work they didn't proofread, or if they shipped whatever the model pooped out on its first go. That is not your work yet. That's what we have to instil. It is OK to draft with AI! Leverage tools, sure - but know the material, make your work your own, and don't ship your first draft.

stories.title_en: Weight-Space Programming builds neural networks like a 1990s researcher

comments.author: noduerme
comments.text:
I love the idea, somehow, that these systems
had to be built
with domain knowledge integrated into the choices of layers and the order of algorithms, using rather brilliant discoveries for optimizing lines and edges, or whatever was relevant to the problem. That's an order of specificity that's lacking from our modern reliance on "one shot" solutions. Letting a one shot solver grind its brains against creating a custom solution to a specific set of transformations is kind if a closing of the circle when it comes to performance and resources for a certain task.
I'm looking forward to the day we can have an optical device that runs only on light input, that looks like a piece of quartz, that you can place over a handwritten number (0-9) and on the top it displays the number in a clean font. Where the neural network to handle this can be translated into physical transformations once it's discovered, no inference processing power required.

comments.author: black3r
comments.text:
The very first referenced issue in that PR discussion sheds a bit more light on this:
https://github.com/adoptium/adoptium-support/issues/1480
This PR's author says there on October 1st: "Got an email from Oracle asking me to NOT proceed with a PR until receiving approval." and then on October 28th: "It's taken over by Oracle. Nothing required from us."

comments.author: dlor
comments.text:
I also found this independently ahead of disclosure and reported it to Oracle last Friday. My harness found it after a fuzzing run and then turned it into a full RCE chain in the target app I was actually scanning.
The harness itself doesn't run with Internet access and I confirmed it didn't access this PR directly, but who knows if this was in the training set itself.
Either way, these simultaneous disclosures are incredibly common now. The Ruby issue affecting Gitlab was not only known about for 6 months, it was publicly fixed for 6 months before someone turned it into an RCE. The fix sat on the Ruby dev branch, and it was never pulled into an actual Ruby release until after Gitlab disclosed their own 10.0 vulnerability through it.
It's very common for reporters to not realize the impact of a bug, models are very good at turning bugs into RCE chains, and the volume everywhere now means security teams are basically only focused on RCEs.
